To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) at local scales, the use of relative wind in the computation of surface fluxes is recommended; (ii) this is true even if the region is not characterized by strong winds; and (iii) this is true also in the presence of a strong mesoscale activity.

(i) at regional and coastal scale, the use of relative wind (i.e., wind corrected for the effect of ocean surface currents) leads to a reduction in heat and momentum flux; (ii) the use of relative instead of geostrophic winds improves the model response especially in terms of SST and in the area characterized by the highest mesoscale activity; (iii) the modification of the original ROMS code to take into account relative winds is cost-less in terms or numerical computation.
surface currents have a significant effect on surface flux computations, which in turn have a large impact on the surface currents and their dynamics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the problem of surface fluxes in the ocean.
the development of a new generation of ocean models, which take into account the impact of surface currents on the computation of the surface fluxes, and the consequent feedback on the dynamics.

the impact, in a temperate region, of the use, in flux computations, of relative winds (instead of absolute winds) and with the feedback, at regional and local scale, of such an improvement on the dynamics of the model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of relative wind in the computation of the surface fluxes, even in a temperate region, should be recommended.

the modification of the code is a good choice for a more reliable model response, even though the impact of the modification is not always evident in terms of quantitative validation with available data.

the use of relative wind is recommended in the computation of surface fluxes, even in the case of a relatively small area (e.g., the Western Mediterranean) and at relatively small spatial scales (e.g., 3 km).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of relative wind is a good practice for coastal applications.
the impact of surface currents on fluxes is important and it is necessary to take it into account in the flux computation, especially in regions where mesoscale and sub-mesoscale activity are strong.
it is important to take into account ocean currents in surface flux computations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the impact of the use of currents in the fluxes is not limited to the dynamics of the currents themselves, but it can be felt on other processes and on other variables, such as the heat budget and its feedback on the dynamics.

, in the presence of a significant mesoscale activity, neglecting the impact of currents on fluxes may lead to an overestimation of the kinetic energy in the surface current field, with a consequent underestimation of the eddy kinetic energy and of the eddy activity.

the impact of currents on flux computations is not negligible, and that it should be taken into account in the computation of surface fluxes in order to improve the model solution, in particular at regional scales.
